comments.content: Missing coverage for a core documented invariant: "recovery never happens after any event reached the caller." The fake-server tests only trigger `previous_response_not_found` and `websocket_connection_limit_reached` before any events are streamed. In `read_ws_events` (src/client/mod.rs) the `!*streamed_any` guards are the only thing preventing a mid-stream retry from replaying the turn and duplicating output already delivered to streaming callers; a regression there (e.g., dropping the flag or resetting it per attempt) would pass the entire current suite. Suggest a scripted-fake-server variant: stream an `output_text.delta`, then send the `previous_response_not_found` (or connection-limit) error envelope, and assert the client surfaces a `ModelError` with no duplicate `response.create` retry frame and no second delta.

comments.content: Inconsistent skip computation: `run_http_stream` uses the raw `session.sent_requests` as the skip point, while every other chained path (`run_ws_turn` at line ~300 and `run_http_turn` at line ~672) routes through `continuation_skip(messages, session.sent_requests)`. `continuation_skip` exists to advance past trailing `ModelResponse` requests (the assistant echo the caller appends to its history after a turn); `history_to_wire` includes ModelResponse items as input whenever `index >= skip`. So on a chained streaming HTTP turn, the previously sent assistant output is re-sent even though the server already has it via `previous_response_id` — the server receives the model output duplicated, which can corrupt the conversation (repeated assistant turns or an invalid input sequence). Fix: use the same helper here.

comments.content: The session `Mutex` is held across the entire SSE read loop, which includes `tx.send(...).await` on the caller-visible mpsc channel. That send applies caller backpressure: if the streaming consumer stops reading the returned stream (a common and legal pattern when the consumer is slow or abandons the stream without dropping it immediately), this lock is never released, deadlocking every subsequent `request`/`request_stream` on the same model — including the server's own ability to make progress. The session state is only touched at terminal events (setting `previous_response_id`/`sent_requests`), so the lock could be scoped tighter, or the sender path could be made non-blocking for the lock holder. Note the same pattern exists in `run_ws_turn` via `ChannelSink`, but there the awaits are on socket reads and the engine's own sink; the HTTP path additionally awaits an unbounded, caller-controlled channel.

comments.content: Inconsistent error handling vs the non-streaming HTTP path: here a non-success status returns `ModelError::http(status, body)` with no `previous_response_not_found` recovery, while `run_http_turn` parses the error code and clears the chain to replay once. The doc comment justifies no replay because "once an event escapes, replaying would duplicate output" — but an HTTP error status arrives before any SSE event is emitted, so a `previous_response_not_found` here is perfectly safe to retry (clear chain, replay full input), and failing instead strands the session: the stale `previous_response_id` stays set, so every subsequent chained turn on this model fails the same way forever. At minimum the stale chain state should be cleared on this error.

comments.content: Both retry loops (`run_ws_turn` here, `run_http_turn` below) retry up to MAX_ATTEMPTS with zero delay. For `RetryKind::Reconnect` this means an immediate reconnect attempt after `websocket_connection_limit_reached` or a socket death — hammering the server during an outage or rate-limit window; for HTTP `previous_response_not_found` it immediately re-posts the full history. A small backoff (even a fixed 100–500 ms, or exponential) between attempts would make retries far less aggressive without violating the "no replay after events escaped" contract.

comments.content: The connection lifetime limit is enforced only between turns and only when `turns_served` is true, so a connection that keeps issuing one turn every `ttl - ε` stays alive indefinitely (and one that never sends a turn is never expired at all). Since the receive loop has no idle/read timeout, an idle client holds the socket, its `SessionResponseCache`, and the forwarder task forever. For a test rig this is minor, but an idle-timeout (e.g. tokio::time::timeout on `ws_rx.next()`) would bound resource retention and make the documented 60-minute lifetime limit actually hold.

comments.content: Timing flakiness: the connection TTL is 50ms, and the test assumes the "early" turn completes its server-side processing before the TTL expires. Under CI load (tokio scheduling, model execution, JSON serialization), the first `run_turn` can legitimately take longer than 50ms, in which case the server would refuse the very first turn with `websocket_connection_limit_reached` and the assertion `events.iter().any(... == "response.completed")` would fail intermittently. Consider using a larger TTL (e.g. 1-2s) with a correspondingly larger sleep, or better, having the rig expose a deterministic way to age out the connection.

comments.content: ResponsesTool::Builtin custom Serialize emits only `{"type": tool_type}` and drops every other field. This type is used in `ResponseObject.tools` (see `ResponseObject::in_progress`, which clones `request.tools`), so a request carrying a hosted tool with configuration (e.g. `{"type":"web_search_preview","search_context_size":"high"}`) is echoed back and persisted as a stripped object. Round-tripping through the response object silently loses the tool configuration, and any later re-serialization of the stored response produces a different wire payload than the client sent. Fix: capture the full JSON value in the Builtin variant (e.g. `Builtin { tool_type: String, fields: serde_json::Map<String, Value> }` or store the raw `Value`) and serialize it back verbatim.

comments.content: `evict_if_full` performs a check-then-act race: the capacity check happens under a read lock, then the write lock is acquired afterwards. Two concurrent `put` calls can both pass the read-lock check and both insert, oversubscribing capacity (eviction then happens on the next put). Additionally, in `SessionResponseCache::put` eviction picks the entry with the minimum `stored_at` wall-clock timestamp; two responses stored in the same instant (likely under load) can evict the wrong one. If the evicted entry is the `previous_response_id` a client chains on, the next turn fails with `previous_response_not_found` spuriously. Fix: do the length check and eviction under the single write lock in `put`, and use a monotonic insertion counter (like `InMemoryResponseStore`'s `seq`) instead of `stored_at` for eviction order.

comments.content: The SSE path has no backpressure or cancellation propagation: it uses an unbounded channel and ignores `start_send` results, so if the HTTP client disconnects mid-stream the spawned task keeps consuming the entire model stream (paying full model cost) with all events silently dropped, and `engine.persist` still records the turn as if it had been delivered. Since this is a test rig, this mainly wastes resources during long streaming tests and can mask disconnect scenarios the tests should exercise. Minimal fix: check `event_tx.is_closed()` in the sink and abort early (returning before persist), or switch to a bounded channel and propagate send failure as a cancellation signal.

comments.content: On a chained turn, only the *new* input items are passed to `input_to_history`, but the `call_names` map used to resolve `function_call_output` → tool name is built exclusively from `function_call` items in that same input. A tool call that was issued on a previous turn (present in the stored history) followed by a `function_call_output` in the continuation therefore produces a `ToolReturnPart` whose `tool_name` is the raw `call_id` string. Backing models that match tool results by tool name will misattribute or reject the result. Fix: thread the already-known call_id→name pairs from the stored history into `input_to_history` (e.g. an optional `known_calls: &HashMap<String, String>` seeded from stored history), or resolve the name from the stored history in `prepare` before converting the new input.

comments.content: `apply_instructions` reorders conversation history on every chained turn regardless of whether instructions changed: it strips system prompts out of *every* stored request and hoists them (or the replacement prompt) into a single leading request. Consequences: (1) system/developer messages that originally appeared mid-conversation are silently moved to the front, which can change model behavior; (2) any stored `ModelRequest` that contained only a system part is dropped entirely from the result (`rest.is_empty()` → not pushed). For the common case (one leading system prompt) this is fine, but the general behavior contradicts the doc comment's implication that "the rest of each request is preserved in order". Minimal fix: only replace the leading system prompt (instructions supplied → drop the first system request and prepend the new one; none supplied → leave history untouched), preserving mid-history system parts and non-empty requests as-is.

comments.content: `part_started` does not guard against a duplicate `PartStart` for an index that already has an open item: `self.open.insert(start.index, ...)` silently overwrites the previous `OpenItem` without emitting its `content_part.done` / `output_item.done` events, and its accumulated text/arguments never reach `completed` / `completed_parts`. A misbehaving or re-splitting model stream then produces a Responses event sequence that never closes the first item (clients assembling items by index will hang or mis-assemble) and the final `response.output` loses the earlier partial item. Minimal fix: in `part_started`, if `self.open.contains_key(&start.index)`, first run `part_ended(&start.index, sequence)` (emitting the done events) before opening the new item.

comments.content: Serializing `ResponsesTool::Function` via `FunctionToolFields` emits `{"name","description","parameters","strict"}` with no `"type":"function"` field, which is invalid Responses-API wire form. Deserialization of that same JSON fails with `missing_field("type")`, so the type does not round-trip. Since `ResponseObject.tools` clones `request.tools` (ResponseObject::in_progress), any server response object containing function tools serializes to a malformed shape that clients/parsers will reject. Fix: include the type tag when serializing, e.g. give FunctionToolFields a `#[serde(rename = "type")] kind: String` set to "function" (or serialize a map with the tag inserted).

Header insertion uses `headers_mut().insert()`, which silently drops any duplicate configured headers (only the last survives). More importantly, `with_header("Host", ...)` etc. would override tungstenite-generated handshake headers; consider at least documenting that configured headers override defaults, or skip/reject Host/Upgrade/Connection/Sec-WebSocket-* keys. Also note `build_request` maps invalid header names/values to `StreamError::Connection`, which is misleading (an invalid configured header is a configuration error, not a connection failure) — minor, but a distinct error variant or message would help diagnosis.
